title: Advocating for Digital Accessibility: An Interview with Junior Fellow Mia Giancola
content:
In this interview, 2026 Library of Congress Junior Fellow Mia Giancola discusses working on the Year of Digital Accessibility in the Library’s IT Design & Development Directorate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Pedro: It’s great to have you on our team this summer. Could you tell us what you are working on?

Mia: Hi! I’m so excited to be here! I’d love to: I am a Junior Fellow working on the Digital Accessibility Team in the Design Division. The Digital Accessibility Team runs an accessibility educational initiative every year called the “Year of.” This year is the “Year of Magnification.” A great way to think of magnification is pinch and zoom, which many people use daily. Magnification is important when considering low vision or blind users, older adults, smartphone users, and several other key populations. In addition to informational materials, I have created an interactive game to help demonstrate the ways magnification can impact how people access digital content, including library resources and collections.

P: Tell us a bit about your background and journey. What professional or educational experiences led you to apply for this fellowship?

title: Transcription Can Bring People Together: A Reflection from Shelby Kruger
content:
Today’s guest post is from Shelby Kruger, a 2026 Junior Fellow at the Library of Congress. Shelby is an M.S.L.S. student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

If I handed you one of Walt Whitman’s early drafts, would you be able to read it? What about a handwritten letter to Abraham Lincoln? Or a diary from the American Revolution? In each of these documents, you might find challenging details to decipher: strange script, S’s that look like F’s, or unknown abbreviations. I encountered each of these elements of historic handwriting during my internship with the Digital Collections Management and Services Division this summer.

title: New Online at the Library of Congress: July 2026
content:
The Library of Congress holds the world’s preeminent body of primary-source materials for the study of the life and work of George and Ira Gershwin, providing a nearly comprehensive record of their music and lyrics, as well as correspondence, photographs, business and financial papers, publicity materials, and press accounts.

This new digital collection primarily features their music (piano-vocal scores, orchestrations, and sketches) and handwritten lyric sheets and librettos. There are also manuscripts, lyric sheets, published sheet music, both concert and theater programs, and at least one self-portrait oil painting of Ira Gershwin smoking a cigarette. What other treasures can you find?

Community Collections Grants from the American Folklife Center supported contemporary cultural field research from 2022-2024. Read more about the program on loc.gov.
